name: chemical-compounds

description.en: 60 common chemical compounds and their formulas: the front is the compound's name in English and Swedish, the back its chemical formula with subscripts (conventional formulas for inorganic compounds, molecular formulas in Hill order for organic compounds). Compiled from Wikidata and PubChem; Swedish names checked against Swedish Wikipedia and, for the less common ones, Svenska Akademiens ordböcker and Swedish official sources.
description.sv: 60 vanliga kemiska föreningar och deras formler: på framsidan föreningens namn på engelska och svenska, på baksidan dess kemiska formel med nedsänkta siffror (gängse formler för oorganiska föreningar, summaformler i Hill-ordning för organiska föreningar). Sammanställd från Wikidata och PubChem; de svenska namnen är kontrollerade mot svenskspråkiga Wikipedia och, för de mindre vanliga, mot Svenska Akademiens ordböcker och svenska myndighetskällor.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (a script comparing each formula's composition, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Candidates: a list of about 70 compounds met in school chemistry and everyday life (acids, bases, salts, oxides, simple hydrocarbons, alcohols, sugars, a few well-known organic compounds) was drawn up by the authoring agent and looked up on Wikidata by exact English label (first query) or by label and alias (second query), requesting the chemical formula (P274), the Swedish label and the PubChem CID (P662). The raw SPARQL JSON responses were saved in the authoring agent's working notes, which are not published; the queries listed below reproduce them. Requests were made with curl and Python urllib with the User-Agent "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)".

Selection: 60 compounds were kept (see Selection). For them the third query fetched every P274 value, all English and Swedish labels and aliases, and the PubChem CIDs. Glucose (Q37525) has no PubChem CID on Wikidata; PubChem CID 5793 (D-Glucose) was used.

Formula on the back: written with Unicode subscript digits. Inorganic compounds, including the carbon compounds conventionally counted as inorganic (CO, CO₂, HCN and the carbonates), use the conventional formula of chemistry teaching (electropositive part first, polyatomic ions kept together: H₂SO₄, NaHCO₃, NH₄NO₃, Ca(OH)₂, HCN), which is Wikidata's P274 value for all of them except HF, HCN and Ca(OH)₂, where Wikidata gives only the Hill-order FH, CHN and CaH₂O₂. Organic compounds use the molecular formula in Hill order (C, H, then other elements alphabetically), exactly as Wikidata's P274 and PubChem give it, e.g. C₂H₆O for ethanol, CH₄N₂O for urea. For ionic compounds the formula is the formula unit (empirical formula), not a molecule.

Formula cross-check: the PubChem PUG REST property table (MolecularFormula, Title, IUPACName) was fetched for all 60 CIDs. PubChem writes formulas in the Hill system (e.g. H2O4S for sulfuric acid), so a comparison script (verify.py, in the unpublished working notes; see Queries) turned each card's formula into element counts (subscript digits read as numbers, each element symbol an upper-case letter optionally followed by a lower-case one, parenthesised groups multiplied by the count after them) and compared those counts with the counts parsed the same way from PubChem's formula and from every Wikidata P274 value of the item (query 3). It also compared the card's exact formula text with the P274 values, the English name case-insensitively with the item's English label and aliases, the Swedish name with its Swedish label and aliases, and resolved the Swedish name on sv.wikipedia (the sitelink and title queries). All 60 matched both in composition; the card's exact text matched a Wikidata P274 value for 57 of 60.

English names: the English front is the compound's common English name, in sentence case. Each was compared case-insensitively with the Wikidata English label and aliases (all 60 matched; acetylsalicylic acid is an alias of the item labelled 'aspirin') and against the PubChem record title. IUPAC spelling 'sulfur'/'sulfate' and 'aluminium' is used.

Swedish names: taken from the Wikidata Swedish label or alias, written in lower case as Swedish common nouns are. Each was resolved on sv.wikipedia through the MediaWiki API (following redirects) and compared with the Wikidata item's sv.wikipedia sitelink: 59 of 60 reached the item's own article, directly or by redirect. Hydrogen chloride (Q211086) has no sv.wikipedia article, and 'väteklorid' redirects to Saltsyra, the article of hydrochloric acid (Q2409), which defines saltsyra as a water solution of väteklorid. Where the label was not the best choice the established name confirmed by sv.wikipedia was used instead: väteklorid (Wikidata has no Swedish label; saltsyra is the solution), kvävemonoxid (Wikidata label 'kväveoxid' is also the generic word for nitrogen oxides), dikväveoxid (systematic; 'lustgas' is in the note), koppar(II)sulfat (alias; label 'Kopparsulfat'), glycerol (label 'propantriol'; sv.wikipedia's article is 'Glycerol'). In quality-control round 2 the less common names were also checked against independent Swedish sources: Svenska Akademiens ordböcker (SAOL and SO, through the JSON search API that the svenska.se site itself calls, found in its JavaScript: https://svenska.se/api/search/{saol|so}?q=<word>&exactMatch=true), Arbetsmiljöverket's limit-value regulation AFS 2023:14 (bilaga 1 lists Väteklorid 'Se saltsyra', Kvävemonoxid, Eten, Vätesulfid) and Läkemedelsverket's product information for medical nitrous oxide ('Dikväveoxid (N2O, medicinsk lustgas)'). SAOL and SO have glycerol, svavelväte, saltsyra, etylen, bikarbonat, lustgas and acetylsalicylsyra; SAOL also has kopparsulfat (neuter: 'ett kopparsulfat') and SO also has vätesulfid; neither has väteklorid, kvävemonoxid or dikväveoxid, which are confirmed by AFS 2023:14 and Läkemedelsverket. Svenska kemisamfundets nomenklaturutskott and NE were not consulted.

Notes: a back note gives a common name from the Wikidata labels or aliases (table salt, baking soda, bikarbonat, quicklime, slaked lime, laughing gas/lustgas, aspirin, ASA, ethene, vätesulfid), or, where Wikidata has no Swedish alias, from the sv.wikipedia article's first sentence (etylen); the solution name for HCl (saltsyra is the Swedish label of Wikidata's hydrochloric-acid item Q2409) and HF; the hydrate for copper(II) sulfate; or, for eight organic compounds, a well-known, commonly taught isomer with the same molecular formula (formulas checked in PubChem and Wikidata), so that the formula-to-name direction has one answer within the deck and the learner knows the formula is not unique in general. Not every isomer is named: only the pairs met in teaching (C₉H₈O₄ is also caffeic acid, which is not mentioned, the card's note being about aspirin).

Machine checks: each card carries a Wikidata check of its formula (P274) where the card's exact text is a Wikidata value, and of its Swedish name where that exact string is a Swedish label or alias; quality control added checks of the isomer isocitric acid's formula (Q288927), the Swedish label 'saltsyra' of hydrochloric acid (Q2409) and the Swedish alias 'vätesulfid' of hydrogen sulfide (Q170591): 110 checks in all, run against live Wikidata by the builder. Formula checks are omitted for hydrogen-fluoride, hydrogen-cyanide, calcium-hydroxide (Wikidata has only the Hill-order string), Swedish-name checks for hydrogen-peroxide, hydrogen-chloride, nitric-oxide, iron-iii-oxide, copper-ii-sulfate, ammonium-nitrate, ethane, glycerol, formaldehyde, urea (Wikidata's string differs only in capitalisation, or the name was chosen over Wikidata's label as described above).

Every card's evidence lists what Wikidata, PubChem and sv.wikipedia showed for it on 2026-10-04, with the opening sentence of the sv.wikipedia article that uses the Swedish name (the article introductions were fetched with the extracts queries below). The deck was built with the builder and validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (node packages/deck-library/scripts/validate_sources.ts chemical-compounds).
selection: 60 common chemical compounds taught in school chemistry or met in everyday life: water and other simple hydrogen compounds (ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen fluoride, hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen cyanide), the common mineral acids, sodium, potassium and calcium salts and hydroxides, magnesium oxide and sulfate, common oxides (of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur, silicon, iron, aluminium, titanium, zinc, calcium, magnesium), copper(II) sulfate, silver nitrate, ammonium nitrate, the simplest hydrocarbons (methane to butane, ethylene, acetylene, benzene), methanol, ethanol, glycerol, formaldehyde, formic, acetic and citric acid, acetone, urea, glucose, sucrose, caffeine, acetylsalicylic acid and chloroform. Inclusion: a single well-defined compound with a Wikidata item carrying P274 and a PubChem record, an established English and Swedish name, and a formula no other card in the deck shares (so the deck can be studied in both directions). Excluded: elements and allotropes (O₂, O₃, N₂), which are not compounds; mixtures and solutions (hydrochloric acid, ammonia water, bleach); hydrates as separate cards (the hydrate is mentioned in a note where it is the familiar form); compounds whose common name is ambiguous between several substances (e.g. 'iron oxide', 'soda'); and, to keep the deck near 60 cards, the further candidates naphthalene, ethylene glycol, toluene, phenol, carbon tetrachloride, sulfur trioxide, ammonium chloride and calcium sulfate. Isomers are not excluded as long as only one of them is in the deck; eight cards name a well-known, commonly taught isomer in a note (not every isomer of every formula is named: C₉H₈O₄, for example, is also caffeic acid).

Its content comes from Wikidata (structured data under CC0 1.0: formulas, labels, aliases) and PubChem (molecular formulas computed by PubChem, a service of the US National Library of Medicine; information created by or for the US government is in the public domain). Only PubChem-computed molecular formulas were used; PubChem record titles, which come from depositor synonyms, were consulted for comparison only and do not appear on the cards. The English names, the formula notation and the notes are the authoring agent's own wording of facts. The selection of compounds was made by the authoring agent, not copied from any list. Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) was used to confirm that each Swedish name is established and refers to the compound; three single names (väteklorid, glycerol and the note name etylen) were first found there because Wikidata lacks them for the item. Single names are facts, not protected expression, so no text, list or selection was copied and the share-alike condition is not triggered; the three names are now also confirmed by independent sources. Arbetsmiljöverket's regulation AFS 2023:14 is a Swedish författning and so not protected by copyright (Copyright Act 9 §). Svenska Akademiens ordböcker and Läkemedelsverket's product information carry no open licence and were used for verification only, nothing copied. No source's licence therefore requires attribution or share-alike, though every source is credited in the deck and this report.

rounds.lens: Sources and machine checks: formula composition against PubChem and Wikidata, names against Wikidata labels and sv.wikipedia, uniqueness of formulas, the builder's live Wikidata checks.
rounds.summary: All 60 formulas agree in composition with PubChem's computed formula and with Wikidata's P274; all English names match a Wikidata label or alias; all Swedish names lead to the item's sv.wikipedia article. No two cards share a formula, so the deck is bidirectional. 107 Wikidata checks pass. The findings record notation and naming differences and how they were resolved.

findings.issue: Wikidata's P274 is only the Hill-order string (FH, CHN, CaH₂O₂), not the conventional HF, HCN, Ca(OH)₂; PubChem likewise gives FH, CHN, CaH2O2.
findings.resolution: Same composition, different notation. The conventional formula is kept (sv.wikipedia also writes HF, HCN and Ca(OH)2); no P274 check for these three cards.

findings.issue: Wikidata Q211086 has no Swedish label and no sv.wikipedia article; 'väteklorid' redirects to the article Saltsyra (hydrochloric acid). PubChem CID 313 is titled 'Hydrochloric Acid'.
findings.resolution: Kept the compound name väteklorid / hydrogen chloride (sv.wikipedia: saltsyra is 'en vattenlösning av ämnet väteklorid') and added a note that its water solution is hydrochloric acid / saltsyra. No Swedish-label check.

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label 'kväveoxid' is also the general word for oxides of nitrogen.
findings.resolution: Used 'kvävemonoxid' (Wikidata alias 'Kvävemonoxid'; sv.wikipedia: 'Kväveoxid eller kvävemonoxid, NO'). No Swedish-label check because the alias is capitalised.

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label is the trivial name 'lustgas'.
findings.resolution: Used the systematic alias 'dikväveoxid' (checked) and put laughing gas / lustgas in the note.

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label is 'propantriol' and it has no Swedish alias 'glycerol'.
findings.resolution: Used 'glycerol', the title of the item's sv.wikipedia article. No Swedish-label check.

findings.card: hydrogen-peroxide, iron-iii-oxide, copper-ii-sulfate, ammonium-nitrate, ethane, formaldehyde, urea
findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label or alias has an initial capital (Väteperoxid, Järn(III)oxid, Koppar(II)sulfat, Ammoniumnitrat, Etan, Formaldehyd, Urea), so an exact label check would fail for the lower-case card text.
findings.resolution: Lower case kept (Swedish common nouns); confirmed by sv.wikipedia; no Swedish-label check for these cards.

findings.issue: Wikidata Q37525 (glucose) has no PubChem CID.
findings.resolution: Compared with PubChem CID 5793 (D-Glucose), formula C6H12O6.

findings.card: ethanol, acetic-acid, acetone, butane, urea, glucose, sucrose
findings.issue: The molecular formula is shared by well-known isomers outside the deck (dimethyl ether, methyl formate, propanal, isobutane, ammonium cyanate, fructose, lactose), so the formula-to-name direction is unique only within the deck.
findings.resolution: Kept the cards (no isomer is in the deck) and named the isomer in a back note; formulas of the isomers checked in PubChem and Wikidata.

findings.card: hydrogen-chloride, hydrogen-fluoride, silicon-dioxide, aluminium-oxide, zinc-oxide, calcium-hydroxide, magnesium-sulfate
findings.issue: PubChem's record titles differ from the card's English name ('Hydrochloric Acid', 'Hydrofluoric Acid', 'Silica', 'Alumina', 'Desitin', 'Calcium;dihydroxide', 'Sulfuric acid magnesium salt (1:1)').
findings.resolution: PubChem titles are depositor-driven preferred names; the English names were confirmed against Wikidata labels and aliases and PubChem's IUPAC names where informative. No change.

rounds.scope: All 60 cards, the description and the selection; formulas re-checked against the NIST Chemistry WebBook and PubChem.
rounds.summary: No factual errors: every formula is correct in composition, every front has one right answer, no two cards share a formula, and the 107 Wikidata checks passed on re-run. Four suggestions: an isomer note for citric acid, the uneven isomer-note policy (caffeic acid), 'carbon compounds' where organic compounds is meant, and loose selection wording. All four were applied (the second by rewording the policy rather than adding a note).

findings.issue: Citric acid's formula C₆H₈O₇ is shared by the well-known isocitric acid (citric acid cycle), but unlike seven other carbon compounds the card names no isomer.
findings.resolution: Verified: PubChem CID 1198 'Isocitric Acid' C6H8O7; Wikidata Q288927 'isocitric acid' P274 C₆H₈O₇, Swedish label 'Isocitronsyra'; sv.wikipedia Isocitronsyra calls the two structural isomers. Added backNote 'Isocitric acid has the same molecular formula.' / 'Isocitronsyra har samma summaformel.', the evidence and a P274 check on Q288927; method and selection now say eight cards.

findings.issue: C₉H₈O₄ is also caffeic acid, so the isomer-note policy is uneven; optional.
findings.resolution: Verified (Wikidata Q56231106 'caffeic acid' P274 C₉H₈O₄, PubChem CID 2518). No note added: the card's note about aspirin/ASA is more useful and caffeic acid is not commonly taught alongside it. The method and selection now say isomer notes are given only for commonly taught pairs, citing C₉H₈O₄/caffeic acid as an example of an isomer not named.

findings.issue: The description says 'molecular formulas for carbon compounds' / 'summaformler för kolföreningar', but CO, CO₂, HCN and the carbonates are carbon compounds written conventionally; the rule is organic vs inorganic.
findings.resolution: Agreed. Description now says 'molecular formulas in Hill order for organic compounds' / 'summaformler i Hill-ordning för organiska föreningar'; method step 4 says inorganic compounds, including the carbon compounds conventionally counted as inorganic (CO, CO₂, HCN, carbonates), use the conventional formula.

findings.issue: The selection promises magnesium hydroxides (no such card) and calls H₂O₂ and HCN 'simple hydrides'.
findings.resolution: Agreed. Selection reworded to 'water and other simple hydrogen compounds (...)' and 'sodium, potassium and calcium salts and hydroxides, magnesium oxide and sulfate'.

rounds.reviewer: Claude (AI) — independent Language and translation reviewer
rounds.scope: All 60 cards plus title, description and keywords; Swedish labels re-fetched from Wikidata.
rounds.summary: Names, language tags, Swedish case and Unicode formulas were found correct. Two warnings (the 'carbon compounds' wording and the thin sourcing of Swedish names) and three note suggestions. The wording was fixed; independent Swedish sources were found and cited (SAOL and SO through svenska.se's search API, Arbetsmiljöverket's AFS 2023:14, Läkemedelsverket's product information); the vätesulfid and bikarbonat notes were changed; the ASA/aspirin note was aligned in English but the Swedish note kept, because Aspirin is a registered trademark in Swedish usage.

findings.issue: The description's 'molecular formulas for carbon compounds' / 'summaformler för kolföreningar' does not match HCN, NaHCO₃, carbonates, CO and CO₂, which are written conventionally.
findings.resolution: Same as round 1: changed to organic compounds / organiska föreningar (with Hill order) in the description and the method.

findings.issue: Swedish names are checked only against Wikidata and sv.wikipedia; väteklorid, kvävemonoxid and glycerol rest on weak ground.
findings.resolution: The SAOL/SO search API behind svenska.se was found in the site's JavaScript and queried (exact match). SAOL and SO list glycerol; SO lists vätesulfid, acetylsalicylsyra; SAOL lists kopparsulfat, saltsyra, etylen, bikarbonat, lustgas, svavelväte. Neither dictionary has väteklorid, kvävemonoxid or dikväveoxid (technical terms), so official sources were used: Arbetsmiljöverket's AFS 2023:14 bilaga 1 lists 'Väteklorid Se saltsyra', 'Kvävemonoxid 10102-43-9', 'Eten', 'Vätesulfid', 'Lustgas'; Läkemedelsverket's product information for medical nitrous oxide reads 'Dikväveoxid (N2O, medicinsk lustgas)'. Wikidata Q2409 (hydrochloric acid) also has the Swedish alias 'Väteklorid'. These are cited in the evidence of hydrogen-chloride, nitric-oxide, nitrous-oxide, glycerol, copper-ii-sulfate, ethylene, hydrogen-sulfide, sodium-bicarbonate and acetylsalicylic-acid and recorded as verification sources; the description now says the less common names were also checked against Svenska Akademiens ordböcker and Swedish official sources. Svenska kemisamfundet and NE were still not consulted, as the method says.

findings.issue: The Swedish front uses the traditional 'svavelväte' while neighbouring cards use systematic names; the systematic 'vätesulfid' is never mentioned.
findings.resolution: Verified: Wikidata Q170591 Swedish alias 'vätesulfid', SO entry 'vätesulfid' = svavelväte, AFS 2023:14 'Vätesulfid'. Added backNote 'In Swedish also called vätesulfid.' / 'Kallas även vätesulfid.' and a Wikidata check of the alias.

findings.issue: The English note (aspirin) and the Swedish note (ASA) carry different facts.
findings.resolution: English note changed to 'Known as aspirin; abbreviated ASA.' (Wikidata English alias 'ASA'). The Swedish note is kept as 'Förkortas ASA.': SO marks 'Aspirin®' as a registered trademark and uses it capitalised as a product name, so calling the substance 'aspirin' in Swedish would name a brand.

findings.issue: The Swedish note 'Kallas även bikarbonat.' differs in style from the bare trivial names used elsewhere.
findings.resolution: Changed to 'Bikarbonat.' (Wikidata Swedish alias 'Bikarbonat'; SAOL entry 'bikarbonat': 'ett av kolsyrans natriumsalter').

rounds.scope: All 60 cards' evidence, the sources, licence evidence, method, queries and licensing; licence pages and queries re-run.
rounds.summary: CC0 compliance confirmed and all quoted evidence verified. Two warnings on documentation (sv.wikipedia supplied some single names although recorded as verification-only; Swedish names rested on linked community sources) and three suggestions (reproducibility, PubChem titles wording, generic sv.wikipedia evidence). All were applied.

findings.issue: Some Swedish names came from sv.wikipedia although it is recorded as verification only, and the method wrongly says the note names came from Wikidata aliases.
findings.resolution: Re-checked on Wikidata (wbgetentities, 2026-10-04): Q151313 and Q132501 have no Swedish aliases, Q211086 no Swedish label; but Q2409 (hydrochloric acid) has Swedish label 'saltsyra' and alias 'Väteklorid', and Q18216 has the alias 'ASA' (English), so saltsyra and ASA do have a CC0 source; Swedish lexemes were also searched (saltsyra and bikarbonat found, none for the others). The names first found on sv.wikipedia are therefore väteklorid, glycerol and etylen. sources.svwiki.usedFor, the Notes step and licensing now say so, explain that single names are facts (no text, list or selection copied, so CC BY-SA does not apply), and record the independent confirmation (AFS 2023:14 for väteklorid, SAOL/SO for glycerol and etylen). Added a Wikidata check of 'saltsyra' on Q2409.

findings.issue: Swedish names rest on Wikidata and sv.wikipedia only, which are linked community sources; the five overridden names were decided by sv.wikipedia alone.
findings.resolution: Independent verification sources added as in round 2: Svenska Akademiens ordböcker (SAOL/SO), Arbetsmiljöverket AFS 2023:14 (public domain under the Copyright Act 9 §) and Läkemedelsverket's product information, each with its licence evidence and cited in the five cards' evidence (kopparsulfat confirmed in SAOL; the card's Stock notation 'koppar(II)sulfat' follows the Wikidata alias).

findings.issue: verify.py, the saved raw responses and the validator command are not reproducible from the record.
findings.resolution: Method step 5 now describes verify.py's algorithm exactly and its command is in queries; step 2 says the raw responses are in the unpublished working notes and are reproduced by the listed queries; the validator command is in queries and step 10. All queries run in this QC pass are listed too.

findings.issue: 'PubChem-computed formulas and record titles' overstates: record titles come from depositor synonyms.
findings.resolution: Verified (CID 14806 titled 'Desitin'). Licensing, sources.pubchem.usedFor and licenseEvidence now say only PubChem-computed molecular formulas were used and record titles were consulted for comparison only, not on cards.

findings.card: water, carbon-dioxide, sulfuric-acid and about 40 others; nitrous-oxide
findings.issue: About 40 cards' sv.wikipedia evidence only records that the article exists; nitrous-oxide's Wikidata evidence repeats a clause.
findings.resolution: The extracts query was run for all 60 articles (three batches, in queries); every opening sentence contains the card's Swedish name, and each generic evidence entry now quotes it (shortened with [...] where long). Duplicate clause removed from nitrous-oxide.

rounds.summary: All formulas, names, notes, the licence decision and the Wikidata checks were confirmed. One misquoted sv.wikipedia fragment (copper-ii-sulfate) and one inaccurate method sentence (hydrogen chloride's sv.wikipedia article) were found; both were verified against the sources on 2026-10-04 and fixed.

findings.issue: The sv.wikipedia evidence quoted '[...] bildar det ett så kallat pentahydrat, CuSO4•5H2O.', but the article says '... varvid det bildar ett så kallat pentahydrat, CuSO4•5H2O.'
findings.resolution: Verified with the extracts API for 'Kopparsulfat' (2026-10-04); the fragment now quotes the source exactly: '[...] varvid det bildar ett så kallat pentahydrat, CuSO4•5H2O.' Card content unchanged.

findings.issue: The method said all 60 Swedish names reached the Wikidata item's own sv.wikipedia article; Q211086 (hydrogen chloride) has no sv.wikipedia sitelink and 'väteklorid' redirects to Saltsyra, the article of Q2409.
findings.resolution: Verified with wbgetentities (Q211086 has no svwiki sitelink; Q2409's svwiki sitelink is 'Saltsyra') and the extracts API ('Väteklorid' redirects to 'Saltsyra', which opens 'Saltsyra, kemisk beteckning HCl(aq) är en vattenlösning av ämnet väteklorid.'). The method now says 59 of 60 reached the item's own article and explains the hydrogen chloride exception, consistent with round 0.

rounds.lens: Final re-check (loop 2): changed cards, every third card, metadata, licence and documentation
rounds.scope: 21 cards (copper-ii-sulfate, changed in round 4, and every third card) against live Wikidata, PubChem, sv.wikipedia, AFS 2023:14, Läkemedelsverket and SAOL/SO; metadata, licence and documentation.
rounds.summary: Every checked formula, name, note, language tag and quoted fragment was confirmed, as were the licence decision and the live Wikidata checks. One documentation warning (method step 7 assigned kopparsulfat and acetylsalicylsyra to the wrong dictionaries) and one Swedish suggestion (neuter agreement in the copper(II) sulfate note) were verified against SAOL/SO on 2026-10-04 and both fixed.

findings.issue: The method said SAOL and SO both have kopparsulfat and that only SO has acetylsalicylsyra; SO has no kopparsulfat, and SAOL has acetylsalicylsyra too. Round 2's resolution assigned the words differently.
findings.resolution: Re-ran the exact-match searches (2026-10-04): both dictionaries have glycerol, svavelväte, saltsyra, etylen, bikarbonat, lustgas and acetylsalicylsyra; kopparsulfat is in SAOL only (SO 0 hits); vätesulfid is in SO only (SAOL 0 hits); väteklorid, kvävemonoxid and dikväveoxid are in neither. The method sentence now says exactly that. Round 2's resolution (which also understated the overlap, e.g. that SO has saltsyra and SAOL acetylsalicylsyra) is kept as the historical record and superseded by this round. No card evidence depended on the wrong assignment (copper-ii-sulfate cites SAOL, which does have kopparsulfat).

findings.issue: The Swedish back note opens 'Vattenfri;', but SAOL gives kopparsulfat neuter gender ('ett kopparsulfat'), so the agreeing form is 'vattenfritt'.
findings.resolution: Verified in SAOL (kopparsulfat and sulfat: 'ett', bestämd form '-et'). The note now reads 'Vattenfritt; de blå kristallerna är pentahydratet CuSO₄·5H₂O.', and the SAOL evidence records the gender.
